The Rite of Spring. Composed by Igor Stravinsky and originally choreographed by Vaslav Nijinsky, The Rite of Spring is a revolutionary 1913 modernist ballet that transformed twentieth-century music and dance. Produced by impresario Sergei Diaghilev as part of his Ballets Russes season in Paris, the work depicts various pagan rituals in ancient Russia celebrating the arrival of spring, culminating in a young girl dancing herself to death as a sacrifice to the god of spring. The visual design was created by the archaeologist and painter Nicholas Roerich, who also co-wrote the scenario. Nijinsky's choreography rejected the classical ballet positions that dominated the art form at the time, instead employing turned-in feet, bent knees, and heavy, stomping movements that shocked audiences accustomed to grace and fluidity. The premiere took place on May twenty-ninth, nineteen thirteen, led by conductor Pierre Monteux, and was met with loud protests, derisive laughter, and physical altercations in the audience, nearly erupting into a riot. The original choreography was lost for decades but was painstakingly reconstructed by Millicent Hodson and Kenneth Archer for the Joffrey Ballet in nineteen eighty-seven. The score itself begins with a famous, extremely high-register bassoon solo playing a Lithuanian folk-inspired melody that sounds alien to Western ears. It is divided into two parts: Adoration of the Earth and The Sacrifice. The Augurs of Spring section features heavy, repetitive, syncopated chords accented by French horns, creating an overwhelming, primitive sound. The final Sacrificial Dance features rapidly shifting time signatures and chaotic accents that exhaust the solo dancer physically. Stravinsky's score introduced polyrhythms, polymeters, and bi-tonality to the orchestral vocabulary, including the famous Rite chord which combines an E-flat dominant seventh with an F-flat major triad. The Rite of Spring is widely regarded as the moment classical music and ballet broke decisively into the twentieth century, establishing a new modernist aesthetic that rejected the Imperial Russian traditions that ballets like Swan Lake and Sleeping Beauty had exemplified.
